See `docs/agents/domain.md`.\\r\\n# CLAUDE.md\\r\\n\\r\\nThis file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Project snapshot\\r\\n\\r\\nLSAT U is a premium ed-tech web app: React 18 + Vite 5 + TypeScript + Tailwind + shadcn/ui, Supabase backend with Edge Functions, hosted on Lovable. The Lovable-connected project is the source of truth; GitHub (`vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db`) is the mirror. Treat the connected project as canonical unless told otherwise.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Second brain (product memory)\\r\\n\\r\\nProduct context, design decisions, pedagogy, and status do NOT live in this repo. They live in the Obsidian vault at `~/ai-os/`. This repo is the code; the vault is the decision layer. Read the vault when starting a session, needing product/design/pedagogy context, or making a decision that touches roadmap or UX. Skip it for trivial code edits.\\r\\n\\r\\nPath sanity check first:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Vault root (the `~/ai-os` directory IS the Obsidian vault): `/Users/joshuaf/ai-os`\\r\\n- Code repo root (this project): `/Users/joshuaf/ai-os/projects/lsatu`\\r\\n\\r\\nIf any older note says `~/Documents/Obsidian Vault/...` or `~/Documents/Claude/02_PROJECTS/LSATU`, treat that as stale — the vault was consolidated into `~/ai-os`. Use the absolute paths above.\\r\\n\\r\\nProtocol is canonical in `~/ai-os/CLAUDE.md` (Session Start / Session End), run via two skills:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **`/pickup`** (start / \\"brief me\\"): reads `wiki/tasks.md` → `wiki/hot.md` → `wiki/dashboard.md` → `wiki/index.md` → latest `wiki/log.md` entry, then gives a 6-8 line briefing (Now / Next / open threads / suggested next) and waits.\\r\\n- **`/wrapup`** (handoff / \\"done for today\\"): proposes which tasks are done (confirm first), strikes them through in `wiki/tasks.md`, refreshes `wiki/hot.md`, appends a dated `wiki/log.md` entry, updates the task anchor, gives a 4-line confirmation.\\r\\n\\r\\n`wiki/tasks.md` is the living ledger of Now / Next / Done; finished work is struck through with a date so a new session never re-runs it.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhere LSATU truth lives in the vault (paths relative to `~/ai-os`):\\r\\n\\r\\nThe vault was rebuilt on 2026-07-16. **Live** pages:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Teaching voice (route ALL student-facing copy through it): `wiki/teaching-voice.md`\\r\\n- The tutoring business (offers, channels, priorities): `wiki/entities/aspiring-attorneys.md`\\r\\n- Hubs: `wiki/tasks.md`, `wiki/hot.md`, `wiki/log.md`, `wiki/dashboard.md`, `wiki/index.md`\\r\\n- A student\'s whole record (transcripts, notes, homework): `students/<name>/` — see `students/README.md` for the primary/mirror rule\\r\\n- LSAT teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md` (fills by ingest)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Archived** — the pre-rebuild product knowledge is read-only reference at `archive/wiki-pre-rebuild-2026-07-16/domains/lsat-u/`; it is not maintained and may be stale. Re-ingest a page through `raw/` if it becomes load-bearing again rather than editing it in place:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Product context: `…/synthesis/intro-to-lr-product.md` (flagship Main Conclusion bootcamp)\\r\\n- Design system (colors, type, role tokens): `…/synthesis/intro-to-lr-design.md`\\r\\n- Code/source map: `…/synthesis/lsatu-source-map.md` (regenerable from this codebase)\\r\\n- Quality bar all bootcamps finish to: `…/synthesis/bootcamp-quality-bar.md`\\r\\n- Concepts, entities, domain index: `…/concepts/`, `…/entities/`, `…/index.md`\\r\\n\\r\\nRules: `raw/` is immutable input, never edit it. Read knowledge from `wiki/`, not `raw/`. Use the `obsidian` CLI (`search`, `backlinks`, `read`) for graph traversal (needs the Obsidian app open); flat file reads work without it. When saving deliverables to the vault, use `[[wiki-link]]` syntax and `UPPERCASE-HYPHENATED.md` naming.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Commands\\r\\n\\r\\nScripts (from `package.json`):\\r\\n\\r\\n- `npm run dev` — Vite dev server on port 8080\\r\\n- `npm run build` — production build\\r\\n- `npm run build:dev` — build with development mode flags\\r\\n- `npm run preview` — serve the built bundle\\r\\n- `npm run lint` — ESLint flat config (`eslint.config.js`)\\r\\n- `npm run test` — Vitest single run (runner wired, no specs exist yet)\\r\\n- `npm run test:watch` — Vitest watch mode\\r\\n- Single test file: `npx vitest run path/to/file.test.ts`\\r\\n\\r\\nPackage manager: **npm**. `package-lock.json` is canonical. A stray `bun.lock` / `bun.lockb` exists in the repo — ignore it, do not switch tooling.\\r\\n\\r\\n- `npm run typecheck` — `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.app.json`. Not optional before a push: `vite build` uses esbuild, which strips types without checking them, so a type error ships and auto-deploys. `.claude/safe-push.sh` gates on this.\\r\\n- `npm run test:e2e` / `npm run playwright` — Playwright e2e (`e2e/smoke.spec.ts`).\\r\\n\\r\\nNo Prettier. Formatting is ESLint-only.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Architecture (big picture)\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Routing** — React Router v6. Routes are registered in `src/App.tsx`, pages live in `src/pages/`. `/foyer` is the landing surface. Feature-gated pages are wrapped by `ProtectedRoute`.\\r\\n- **Auth + permissions** — Supabase Auth session plus Lovable Cloud Auth JWT fallback (`@lovable.dev/cloud-auth-js`). Per-feature access flags (`has_practice_access`, `has_drill_access`, `has_chat_access`, `is_admin`, ...) are resolved in `src/hooks/useUserPermissions.ts`. Session death is detected via JWT/401.\\r\\n- **Supabase integration** — client auto-generated at `src/integrations/supabase/client.ts` (Supabase JS v2). DB types are auto-generated — do not hand-edit. Edge Functions (Deno) in `supabase/functions/`: `admin-manage-users`, `analyze-stem-response`, `generate-micro-drill`, `motivation-engine`, `parse-drill-request`, `tutor-chat`, `voice-coach-respond`. SQL migrations in `supabase/migrations/`.\\r\\n- **State** — React Context for cross-cutting concerns (`AuthContext`, `UserSettingsContext`, `QuestionBankContext`, `ThemeContext`, `TimerContext`). TanStack Query v5 for server state.\\r\\n- **Primary navigation — Foyer** — `src/pages/AcademyFoyer.tsx` composes `src/components/foyer/FoyerSidebar.tsx` (state blocks + workspace nav) with `src/components/foyer/FoyerHeroRing.tsx` (3 nodes: Smart Drill, Resume, Ask Joshua). This is the primary nav for the product.\\r\\n- **Messaging / Inbox** — real messaging feature, not cosmetic. Lives in `src/components/inbox/` (`FloatingMessenger`, `ConversationView`, `ThreadList`) plus `src/hooks/useInbox.ts`. One ongoing 1:1 thread per student with the admin (Joshua). Supports PDF attachments. Gated by `has_chat_access`.\\r\\n- **Practice surfaces** — Drill and Wrong Answer Journal (WAJ) are real product surfaces, not launchers. Core logic in `src/lib/`: `adaptiveEngine`, `drillIntelligence`, `achievementEngine`, `gamification`, `questionLoader`, `streakSystem`, `wajService`.\\r\\n- **Admin** — `AdminDashboard` + `admin-manage-users` edge function. Must be desktop AND mobile responsive. Needs granular per-feature toggle control.\\r\\n- **UI primitives** — shadcn/ui (Radix + `class-variance-authority`) in `src/components/ui/`. Icons from `lucide-react` and `@tabler/icons-react`. Framer Motion for animation. Spline for 3D.\\r\\n- **Styling** — Tailwind 3.4 over HSL custom properties in `src/index.css`, surfaced as tokens in `tailwind.config.ts`. `DESIGN.md` is the visual authority; `.impeccable/design.json` is its machine-readable sidecar. Prefer tokens over ad-hoc hex values, and never add a token name whose CSS variable is not defined - three such names (`accent-bronze`, `accent-warm`, `glow-bronze`) shipped broken for five months and silently removed the focus ring from every shared Button.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Conventions\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Git workflow:** Always commit and push directly to `main`. Never create feature branches or pull requests unless explicitly asked. On 2026-09-27 an accidental \\"revert and resend\\" (b998596) silently undid three merged PRs across 121 question-bank files, and students saw the wrong questions again. To undo your own work, `git revert <your SHA>` only. Do not flip these without explicit approval — it would cascade into a very large diff.\\r\\n- Lovable-specific plumbing that must not be removed:\\r\\n  - `lovable-tagger` Vite plugin injects `data-lov-id` in dev\\r\\n  - `vite-plugin-pwa` configured with start URL `/foyer`\\r\\n  - Lovable preview Service Worker guard in `src/main.tsx`\\r\\n- Identity rules: email sign-in, profile identity uses **name** (not username), instructor is displayed as **\\"Joshua\\"**, students display their real profile names.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Cross-tool instruction hygiene\\r\\n\\r\\n`CLAUDE.md` is the fuller project source of truth. `AGENTS.md` is the Codex-facing adapter and should stay aligned without becoming a second full copy.\\r\\n\\r\\n- When updating project instructions, update both files as needed: put durable detail here, and keep `AGENTS.md` as a concise adapter.\\r\\n- When creating a Claude skill that Codex should use, also copy it to `.agents/skills/` with its `SKILL.md` and supporting files.\\r\\n- When creating a Claude agent that Codex should spawn, also create a matching `.codex/agents/<name>.toml` and place the converted instructions in `developer_instructions`.\\r\\n- When adding shared knowledge, put it in `docs/`, `references/`, or `templates/` so every tool can read the same source.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Verification (must not skip)\\r\\n\\r\\nAny change to `src/components/` or `src/pages/` is not \\"done\\" until it has been viewed running in the app (dev server + browser tool, e.g. Playwright or chrome devtools MCP), with a screenshot or DOM check as evidence. Do not report a UI change complete on the strength of the diff alone. A responsive defect that gets pushed as \\"fixed\\" and does not hold costs a second full session — this has already happened (a pushed Home-page fix that did not survive, then 13 screenshots and 8 emulate cycles to actually close it). One matrix pass before the push is cheaper than either.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Product rules (must not regress)\\r\\n\\r\\n- Foyer (`FoyerSidebar` + `FoyerHeroRing`) is the primary navigation. The Foyer additionally hosts a `GooeyDock` quick-launch row well below the orbital ring; this dock is allowed only on `/foyer`. Do not add docks elsewhere.\\r\\n- Inbox is real messaging with back-and-forth threads and PDF attachments, scoped 1:1 per student with admin.\\r\\n- Admin is fully responsive on desktop and mobile.\\r\\n- Do not expose actions users cannot actually perform — no fake analytics, no dead buttons, no misleading placeholders. Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n**LSAT teaching standard, selected 2026-10-02:** Joshua chose the supplied Conditional Reasoning transcription as the reference for how LSAT material should sound and unfold. Read [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md) before drafting lessons, notes, explanations, drills, flashcards, quizzes, or instructional feedback. It contains the detailed source analysis, original calibration examples, progression, and review rubric. [Source identity and limits](sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) are preserved separately. This choice develops the teaching-content register below; correspondence and marketing retain their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Air between ideas. Real correspondence is short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters). In teaching, vary sentence and paragraph length with the reasoning: give an explanation room, then let a short sentence settle the consequence. Do not impose email brevity on a lesson or cut its intermediate reasoning.\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\"; \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs: never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. The indicator is bold; the complete idea it refers to is in brackets.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p><strong>If</strong> [you win the raffle], you get a bicycle.</p><p>You get a bicycle <strong>if</strong> [you win the raffle].</p><span>If identifies the sufficient condition in both sentences.</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>In the second sentence, if appears in the middle. Its condition comes last, but winning is still enough to establish getting a bicycle. Don\'t let the first phrase in English choose the first side of your diagram.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"You get a bicycle if you win the raffle. Which diagram preserves this sentence?\\" options={[\'Get bicycle → Win\', \'Win → Get bicycle\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You let sentence order choose the arrow. The if-clause still makes winning enough for getting a bicycle.\', \'The sufficient condition is still winning. Where it appears in the sentence does not change what it establishes.\']}/>\\r\\n    </div>\\r\\n  </section>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n// One translation process, checked four ways, instead of five restarted lessons.\\r\\nfunction WholeMeaningNote() {\\r\\n  const onlyComparison = groupSection(\'group-2\', \'Compare only with the only\');\\r\\n  const insideCheck = Children.toArray(reference(12).props.children);\\r\\n  return <>\\r\\n    <NoteSection title=\\"Check a translation four ways\\">\\r\\n      <p>A diagram can point the right way and still say the wrong thing. Each check below catches a different slip in the same translation process.</p>\\r\\n      <ol>\\r\\n        <li><strong>Target:</strong> did you find the whole idea the indicator refers to, wherever it sits?</li>\\r\\n        <li><strong>Qualification:</strong> did your short label keep every restriction?</li>\\r\\n        <li><strong>Direction:</strong> did a similar-looking expression trick you into the wrong side?</li>\\r\\n        <li><strong>Imagined case:</strong> does your arrow promise something the sentence leaves open?</li>\\r\\n      </ol>\\r\\n    </NoteSection>\\r\\n    <NoteSection title=\\"Check 1: find the whole target, wherever it sits\\">\\r\\n      <p>An indicator\'s <strong>target</strong> is the complete word or phrase it refers to. In “All guests wearing blue badges receive vouchers,” all refers to guests wearing blue badges, not guests alone.</p>\\r\\n      <p>The target often comes after its indicator. ## assistant

Use an explicit opening-path classifier:

- `/lessons`, excluding `/lessons/:unitId`
- `/opening/:stepId`
- `/opening-practice`, `/opening-labs`, `/opening-tools`

  and why. Don't hand back a plan when the work was asked for.
- **Look before asking.** If the answer is on disk or reachable through a connected tool,
  go get it. He has Firecrawl, Google Workspace (`gws`), and `gh` — use them.
- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step
  failed or was skipped, lead with that. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I
  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill
  and apply it in that turn, whatever else is in progress.

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

## Safety

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted
  and shown to him. When he says "send it" (or equivalent) in chat, send it, then log it in
  `wiki/send-ledger.md`. Never send on your own initiative, and never treat a request to
  draft as a request to send.
- **Never delete** files, emails, or records without explicit confirmation.
- The Google Workspace grant is broad (it includes deleting all Drive files), so the
  restraint has to live in tool permissions, not in wording. A prompt is not a permission
  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or
  a chat.

## Tools already connected

- **Firecrawl** — CLI + 28 skills. Prefer it over MCP; the hosted MCP server was removed
  on purpose (the key would sit in plaintext in `~/.Codex.json`).
- **Google Workspace** — `gws` CLI, GCP project `ai-os-joshua`. Gmail, Calendar, Drive,
  Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, People.
- **GitHub** — `gh` CLI, authenticated.

## Cost discipline

`AGENTS.md` reloads on every message, so keep this file lean. Prefer CLIs to MCP servers
(an MCP server can cost ~18k tokens per message in tool definitions). `/clear` between
unrelated tasks. Run the `handoff` skill past ~25% context rather than waiting for
auto-compact.

point of the file.*

# Jay 2 — operating instructions for Codex (ai-os)

The canonical root is the repository directory containing this file (`C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` on this Windows machine). Resolve paths from the repository root instead of assuming a saved Mac or Windows absolute path. This is the router: it holds pointers, not knowledge. Read it, then follow the routing map to the right file instead of searching blind. Twin for Claude Code: `CLAUDE.md`.

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

Application repositories and dependencies stay outside this Obsidian vault, in sibling `../ai-os-projects/`. Do not create a junction from the vault back into that directory.

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**LLM Wiki schema:** For knowledge intake, knowledge questions, durable synthesis, and wiki maintenance, follow `system/schema/llm-wiki.md`. Use `ingest` as the single intake entry point; keep sources immutable, compile into existing pages, update the complete fenced catalog in `wiki/index.md`, and append changes to `wiki/log.md`. Preserve domain homes and live-system authority. Mechanical tasks retain the retrieval exceptions above.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **LSAT teaching:** use project-owned `lsat-u-voice` and `references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md`; this Joshua-selected standard takes precedence over older vendor voice blends.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

## Tools, keys, and secrets

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). OAuth client secrets live in `~/.config/gws/`, outside the repo. There is no vault, no Keychain, no encrypted store (`records.sparsebundle` is dead) and none is wanted. Never paste a credential into chat — add it to `.env` directly in the editor.
- **Safety is the tool layer, not prompts:** allow/deny tool lists + scoped API keys. Jay 2 acts under its own credentials and never impersonates Joshua.
- **Connected live systems:** Cal.com, Google Calendar, LSAT U Supabase, Stripe, Gmail. Full registry in `connections.md`.
- **Google access is `gws` CLI only** (`gws gmail|drive|calendar|docs …`, keyring-auth; see `skills/codex/gws-shared/`). Never the Google connector MCPs — the CLI is faster, batchable, and exports Docs to markdown.
- **Shared Windows command tools:** use `uv`, `yt-dlp`, `ffmpeg`, `ffprobe`, `ffplay`, and `deno` from the Windows user PATH. For versions, locations, how to invoke them, or a stale terminal environment, read `references/ai-workspace/windows-cli-toolchain.md`. Check before reinstalling; restart the affected IDE when its inherited PATH is stale.
- **Government IDs stay outside this OS.** Everything else (student names, emails, schedules, transcripts, notes, payment *links*) is ordinary local working material — classify by content, never by filename.
- **Git remote is enabled.** `origin` is GitHub (`vnjkoxpl-42905/ai-os`, decided 2026-09-29). The outer repo never tracks `.env`, `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/` (own repo), runtime logs, or locks. Do not create gitlinks.

Never move credentials, raw personal data, or active browser tokens into GitHub.

Joshua explicitly authorized credential transfer; implementation uses the authenticated encrypted package described in `setup/github-sync/README.md`; plaintext secrets and its unlock key stay outside GitHub and Drive. Cloud authentication and native browser sessions still require separate verification.

## Skills

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. An item runs only once **activated by copy** (not symlink) into `.agents/skills/` (Claude: `.claude/skills/`). Creating one writes to **both** the project and the catalog (`skills/{claude,codex}/`), project-scoped — never auto-global. `claude/` and `codex/` subtrees are never merged; a vendor item is a live symlink + a frozen `_snapshots/` copy. `system/scripts/check-skills.sh` validates the model; `skills/INDEX.md` indexes it.

Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `pickup` / `wrapup` | `pickup` only on Joshua's explicit request / `wrapup` at session end (wrapup persists to the wiki ledgers) |
| `session-handoff` | mid-work context reset near ~250k, or passing work Codex↔Claude — chat-only, writes nothing |
| `audit` | scoring the OS against the Four Cs (structural health, /100) |
| `level-up` | weekly 3Ms interview to find + ship one automation |
| `consultation-inquiry-drafts`, `-followup-drafts`, `inbound-tutoring-replies` | drafting to prospects/students — always via the teaching voice |
| `guided-drill-assignment` | assigning a student a drill |

When a skill run exposes a gap, improve the skill before moving on. Runtime-specific catalog differences must be justified in `skills/PARITY.md`; undeclared differences are defects.

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Lovable credits require confirmation.** Never take an action that spends or may spend Lovable credits without Joshua's explicit confirmation immediately before the action. Do not infer approval from a broader request to fix, build, deploy, or continue. Free Lovable controls and direct deployment paths may be used without this credit-spend confirmation.
- **Lovable Cloud deploys through Lovable.** LSAT U currently uses a Lovable Cloud-managed backend. Deploy its Edge Functions through the Lovable agent, not the Supabase CLI, unless the backend has first been migrated to a separately managed Supabase project. Confirm this route with Joshua before starting a Lovable deployment.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.
- Activated skills are **copies** in `.agents/skills/` (from `skills/codex/`); agent definitions convert to `.codex/agents/*.toml` with the instructions in `developer_instructions`.
- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.
- Activation is unequal by design: Codex reads copies in `.agents/skills/`, Claude reads copies in `.claude/skills/`. Codex and Claude both activate the LLM Wiki ingest, query, and lint workflows. Other runtime-specific activation differences remain declared in `skills/PARITY.md`. Never have separate runtimes writing the same page concurrently.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 1.2 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"d71944","wall_time_seconds":0.4089527,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":5186,"output":"}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function conditionalReferenceContent() {\\r\\n  return <div className=\\"cr-sequence\\">\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={1} label=\\"Start with meaning\\" title=\\"What does a conditional tell you?\\">\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>condition</strong> is an idea that can be true or false. You win a raffle. You get a bicycle. We can ask whether either condition holds in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>conditional statement</strong> tells us that if one condition is true, another has to be true too. It gives us a rule we can use, even before we know whether either condition is true in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p className=\\"co-if-inline\\">We aren\'t saying the first condition happened. We\'re asking what would follow <strong>if</strong> it did.</p>\\r\\n      <HypotheticalFigure/>\\r\\n      <h3>Why learn this?</h3><p>On the LSAT, you need to distinguish what the information proves from what it leaves open. A conditional rule can help you prove a conclusion. An argument can also misuse the rule and reach a conclusion it hasn\'t proved. We\'ll practice telling those apart.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Let\'s read one rule.</p><blockquote>{raffleRule}</blockquote>\\r\\n      <p>Under this rule, winning the raffle makes getting a bicycle certain. Winning without getting one would break the stated relationship. That is what we mean by a <strong>guarantee</strong> here.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Compare that with “If you win the raffle, you usually get a bicycle.” Usually allows an exception. Our rule does not. Take the stated rule as given; we are asking what it tells us, not whether a real organizer keeps a promise.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Does the rule itself tell us that you actually win the raffle?\\" options={[\'Yes, it says I win.\', \'No, it tells me what follows if I win.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You added a case fact. The rule has not reported a win; it tells you what getting one would establish.\', \'Imagining a win helps us understand the rule. We need a separate fact to establish that you actually win.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now let\'s take the two conditions one at a time.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={2} label=\\"Sufficient means enough\\" title=\\"One condition gives you enough\\">\\r\\n      <blockquote>{raffleRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>if-part</strong> is the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>. Sufficient means enough. Knowing you win is enough, under this rule, to know you get a bicycle.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-role-exhibit\\"><span>Sufficient</span><strong>Win the raffle</strong><p>Enough to establish getting a bicycle</p></div>\\r\\n      <p>You might win. You might not. The rule has not settled that question.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"You don\'t win the raffle. Could you still get a bicycle?\\" options={[\'Yes. Getting a bicycle is still possible.\', \'No. Without winning, getting a bicycle is impossible.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'You could buy one or receive one as a gift. You could also not get one. Neither case creates a winner who fails to get a bicycle, so both fit the rule.\', \'You made winning the only way to get a bicycle. The sentence gives one sufficient condition; it has not excluded other ways.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now suppose a fact gives us the sufficient condition. That is when we can <strong>use</strong>, or activate, the rule in its stated direction.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"You win the raffle. Do we need another fact to establish that you get a bicycle?\\" options={[\'Yes, we need another fact about the bicycle.\', \'No, the rule and the win establish it.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'The rule already covers the case in which you win. That fact meets its sufficient condition.\', \'Winning meets the sufficient condition. With the rule, that is enough to establish that you get a bicycle.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>We\'ll now keep this job in mind while changing the wording.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={3} label=\\"The sufficient family\\" title=\\"Different words can preserve the same rule\\">\\r\\n      <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is an expression that helps you recognize a conditional relationship. These expressions can introduce an idea that is enough to establish another.</p>\\r\\n      <p>For the next examples, use a different stated rule: anyone who borrows a locker has a key. We will express that same connection in several ways. We haven\'t said everyone with a key borrows a locker.</p>\\r\\n      <WordFamily entries={sufficientFamily} role=\\"sufficient\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>When/whenever and any/anytime group related forms together. An ending changes the kind of case being discussed, but these examples keep the same connection. For example, every guest wearing a blue badge covers that whole group. Guest alone would include people without badges. Use the expression to find the group, then keep the words that limit it.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Every guest wearing a blue badge receives a lunch voucher. Which complete idea is enough?\\" options={[\'Guest\', \'Guest wearing a blue badge\', \'Receives a lunch voucher\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Guest alone drops the badge restriction and would make a claim about unbadged guests.\', \'The rule gives a voucher to every guest wearing a blue badge. Keep that qualification with the person.\', \'The voucher is what the rule establishes. It has not said every voucher recipient wears a blue badge.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>Two more Group 1 expressions</summary><p><strong>Where</strong> can state a relationship across locations: “Where a collection point operates, parcels can be returned.” An operating collection point establishes the availability of returns there. Availability is not proof that someone made a return.</p><p><strong>The only</strong> needs its complete phrase: “The only notebooks on this shelf are hardback.” A notebook on the shelf is hardback. The sentence does not put every hardback notebook there.</p><p>These are part of your Group 1 work. Understand what the full expression covers before using its group as a placement shortcut.</p></details>\\r\\n      <p>We have seen what can be enough. Now let\'s name what that condition requires.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={4} label=\\"Necessary means required\\" title=\\"The other condition has to be there\\">\\r\\n      <blockquote>{raffleRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>then-part</strong> is the <strong>necessary condition</strong>. Necessary means required. Under this rule, if you win, getting a bicycle has to follow.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-role-exhibit cr-required\\"><span>Necessary</span><strong>Get a bicycle</strong><p>Required whenever you win the raffle</p></div>\\r\\n      <p>Ask “required for what?” Here, a required result of winning under this rule. It is not a requirement you must satisfy before entering. The word necessary describes the relationship, not when the events occur.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We\'re looking at the same rule from its other side. Winning is enough to establish getting a bicycle. Getting a bicycle is the result the rule requires whenever you win.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Under our rule, what has to follow if you win?\\" options={[\'You get a bicycle.\', \'You ride the bicycle home.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Getting a bicycle is the stated result. Winning without getting one would violate the rule.\', \'Riding is not part of this rule. The sentence establishes that you get a bicycle, not what you do with it.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Necessary does not mean “the next event.” It means required by this relationship. A conditional need not tell you which event caused another, or when either happened.</p>\\r\\n      <p>As with sufficient language, the wording can vary while the relationship stays the same.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={5} label=\\"The necessary family\\" title=\\"Listen for what the sentence needs\\">\\r\\n      <p>Return to our locker rule. Borrowing a locker requires a key. The next expressions all identify that requirement in their complete sentences.</p>\\r\\n      <WordFamily entries={necessaryFamily} role=\\"necessary\\"/>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-contrast\\"><div><h3>If</h3><p>“You borrow a locker <strong>if</strong> you have a key.”</p><p>Having a key is enough for borrowing under this sentence.</p></div><div><h3>Only if</h3><p>“You borrow a locker <strong>only if</strong> you have a key.”</p><p>Having a key is required. This sentence has not made it enough.</p></div></div>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"A guest enters the lounge only if the guest has a current pass. What does entering establish?\\" options={[\'The guest has a current pass.\', \'Every guest with a pass enters.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Only if identifies the current pass as required for entry. An entering guest therefore meets that requirement.\', \'You made the requirement enough. A guest could have a current pass and remain outside without violating the sentence.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>More Group 2 forms, with the sentence intact</summary><p><strong>Only when</strong> and <strong>only where</strong> can restrict the occasions or places of an outcome: “The fountain runs only when its pump is on.” A running fountain requires an operating pump. The pump being on does not establish that the fountain runs.</p><p><strong>Requires</strong> directly names a requirement: “Entry requires a current pass.” Preserve current. <strong>Always</strong> needs the sentence\'s subject and scope: “The upstairs room is always quiet when the door is shut.” Here a shut door establishes quiet, not the other way around.</p><p><strong>Only</strong> and <strong>the only</strong> are different complete expressions. “Only people who get a bicycle win this raffle” and “The only people who win this raffle are people who get a bicycle” both preserve the rule: winning establishes getting a bicycle.</p></details>\\r\\n      <p>We can now recognize both roles before writing any symbols. Next, let\'s see what happens when a requirement is missing.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={6} label=\\"A missing requirement\\" title=\\"What if the requirement is missing?\\" dark>\\r\\n      <ContrapositiveDiscovery/>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={7} label=\\"The four situations\\" title=\\"Keep what follows separate from what stays open\\">\\r\\n      <p>Change the fact about your outcome while keeping the rule. Treat each fact as settled, not as a report that you are still waiting. Decide what it establishes before comparing the explanation.</p>\\r\\n      <FourCaseExplorer/>\\r\\n      <p>Starting from getting a bicycle and concluding that you win is the tempting <strong>reverse</strong>. Starting from not winning and concluding that you do not get a bicycle is the tempting <strong>inverse</strong>. Neither follows from this rule alone.</p>\\r\\n      <p>The contrapositive starts from <strong>not getting a bicycle</strong> and establishes <strong>not winning the raffle</strong>. Its reasoning depends on the missing required result, not on reversing whichever words happen to appear.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We now understand the relationship in words. Symbols will let us record that understanding without carrying every word of the sentence.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={8} label=\\"Build the first diagram\\" title=\\"Give the relationship a shorter form\\">\\r\\n      <p>Put the sufficient condition on the <strong>left</strong>, the necessary condition on the <strong>right</strong>, and a <strong>must arrow</strong> between them.</p>\\r\\n      <RuleDiagram left=\\"Sufficient: enough\\" right=\\"Necessary: required\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>The arrow means the left condition requires the right. It does not mean the left caused the right, or that the right happens later.</p>\\r\\n      <h3>Which idea goes on which side?</h3>\\r\\n      <p>The indicator helps you find a condition\'s job. Once you\'ve found that job, place the <strong>complete condition</strong> on its side of the arrow. We don\'t put the word if or only if in the diagram.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-contrast\\"><div><h3>Left: sufficient</h3><p>This is the condition that\'s enough to establish the other one. Group 1 expressions such as <strong>if, when, all, every</strong> and <strong>any</strong> can identify this condition.</p><p>“All people who borrow a locker have a key.” All refers to <strong>people who borrow a locker</strong>. For someone in that group, having a key follows. Borrowing goes left.</p></div><div><h3>Right: necessary</h3><p>This is what the sufficient condition requires. Group 2 expressions such as <strong>only if, requires</strong> and <strong>must</strong> can identify the requirement.</p><p>“Borrowing a locker requires a key.” What is required? <strong>Having a key.</strong> That condition goes right.</p></div></div>\\r\\n      <RuleDiagram left=\\"Borrows a locker\\" right=\\"Has a key\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>Read it back: if someone borrows a locker, they have a key. The roles stay the same.</h3>\\r\\n      <p>Compare these two versions of our raffle rule. The indicator is bold; the complete idea it refers to is in brackets.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p><strong>If</strong> [you win the raffle], you get a bicycle.</p><p>You get a bicycle <strong>if</strong> [you win the raffle].</p><span>If identifies the sufficient condition in both sentences.</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>In the second sentence, if appears in the middle. Its condition comes last, but winning is still enough to establish getting a bicycle. That condition still goes left. Don\'t let the first phrase in English choose the first side of your diagram.</p>\\r\\n      <RuleDiagram left=\\"Win the raffle\\" right=\\"Get a bicycle\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>Now try the same move with a requirement.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p><strong>Only</strong> [people with a key] borrow a locker.</p><p>A person borrows a locker <strong>only if</strong> [they have a key].</p><span>Only and only if identify the necessary condition here.</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>Both sentences say locker borrowers have a key. In the first, only is at the beginning. In the second, only if is in the middle. Having a key is required in both, so it goes right. <strong>If</strong> and <strong>only if</strong> have different jobs; read only if as the whole expression.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"A person borrows a locker only if they have a key. Which condition goes on the right?\\" options={[\'Borrows a locker\', \'Has a key\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Borrowing is what has the requirement. Ask what a locker borrower must have: a key. Borrowing goes left; having a key goes right.\', \'Having a key is required for borrowing. Only if appears in the middle, but it still identifies the necessary condition.\']}/>\\r\\n      <h3>The indicator can also follow its target</h3>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p>[Having a key] is <strong>required</strong> for borrowing a locker.</p><p>Borrowing a locker <strong>requires</strong> [having a key].</p><span>Having a key is the requirement in both sentences.</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>The target is the complete idea the indicator refers to. It comes before required in the first sentence and after requires in the second. Having a key still goes right. We find it by asking what is required, not by taking whichever words come next.</p>\\r\\n      <p>In your Group 1 and Group 2 lessons, compare what each expression tells you about the same case. If you know someone borrows a locker, a key follows. Knowing that person has a key leaves borrowing open. Different wording should preserve that distinction.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Let\'s build an original diagram slowly. Its job has not changed.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Which diagram preserves the moved if-clause?\\" options={[\'Get bicycle → Win\', \'Win → Get bicycle\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You let sentence order choose the arrow. The if-clause still makes winning enough for getting a bicycle.\', \'The sufficient condition is still winning. Where it appears in the sentence does not change what it establishes.\']}/>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={9} label=\\"Write and read the contrapositive\\" title=\\"Write the meaning you already understand\\">\\r\\n      <p>Win means you win the raffle. Write that as <strong>~Get bicycle → ~Win</strong>. The <strong>~</strong> sign means <strong>not</strong>. First make the relationship accurate. The code contains **two connected but different curriculum surfaces**: the revised opening course has **9 notes and 4 drills**; the recorded full curriculum has **30 units, 296 drill questions, and 30 guided examples**. The revised opening course does not yet carry its new page structure through the later units.

The exact opening order is defined in [openingCoursePath.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/openingCoursePath.ts:13). Its actual content is composed in [OpeningCourseContent.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/OpeningCourseContent.tsx:255).

| Order | Destination | Actual teaching and checks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **What conditionals are** | A condition can hold or fail. A conditional gives a rule, not a report that its starting condition occurred. The raffle example distinguishes a guarantee from “usually.” Inline check asks whether reading the rule establishes a win. |
| 2 | **The sufficient condition** | Sufficient means enough, rather than the only possible route. Checks whether a nonwinner could receive a bicycle and whether a known win needs another fact to establish the bicycle. |
| 3 | **The necessary condition** | Necessary means required by the relationship, rather than earlier in time or a guarantee of the sufficient condition. Checks the precise required result and whether receiving a bicycle establishes winning. |
| 4 | **Enough, required, or still open?** | **Dedicated instruction page:** read the rule and supplied facts, decide what follows, inspect feedback and retry. **Exercise:** seven progressive tasks covering rule versus fact, applying a new fact, identifying sufficient/necessary roles, an absent sufficient condition, other possible causes, and a counterexample to reversal. |
| 5 | **Read the must arrow** | Sufficient left, necessary right; arrow means “must,” without implying cause or chronology. Incrementally builds the raffle diagram. Checks a moved if-clause so English word order cannot determine arrow direction. Foundation recall cards follow. |
| 6 | **Sufficient-condition words** | Two concept introductions, then seven expression explanations: **if, when, where, all, the only, every, any**. Covers complete subjects, qualified conditions, clause position, each/whenever variants, definite-result language such as ensures/implies, and words used outside conditional statements. Learner moves through expressions or revisits them; explanation reveals, supplementary wording and recall cards support review. |
| 7 | **Build the sufficient side** | **Dedicated instruction page:** identify the complete sufficient condition, diagram/read back, then construct a case exposing reversal. **Exercise:** target-selection lab, sentence-to-diagram builder, the-only distinction, equivalent-rule check with optional recall cards, and a constructed counterexample. It uses a task runner; individual labs can contain several examples. |
| 8 | **Necessary-condition words** | Seven expression explanations: **only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires, must**. Includes requirement-before/after wording, strict depends-on/relies-on language, and whole-expression interpretation. Adds an only/only-if side check, supplementary wording and recall cards. A separate boundary explains why permission and instructions cannot become reports of actual conduct. |
| 9 | **Keep the whole meaning** | Four checks: find the complete target wherever it appears; retain qualifications; distinguish only/the only; test an interpretation through a possible case. Interactive target readers, applicant/pass qualification choices, an only/the-only comparison check, and inside-the-sentence testing put these checks into use. |
| 10 | **Conditional translation practice** | **Dedicated minimal landing:** purpose, Start practice, session-save notice. **Exercise:** separate briefing before each stage, then one question at a time: 3 qualification checks → 7 reviewed diagram-engine items → 6 independent written translations/readbacks before comparison → 4 equivalent-rule comparisons → 4 fresh transfer questions. Mistakes produce up to four distinct fresh checks. First checks and corrections remain separate in the summary. |
| 11 | **When a requirement is missing** | Derives the missing-required-result inference before giving its notation. Four-case explorer distinguishes forward inference and contraposition from reverse/inverse errors. Explicitly separates what is established from what remains open. |
| 12 | **Write and read the contrapositive** | Reverse and negate both complete conditions; cancel existing negatives. Four sign patterns and the five-step translation routine. Practical questions cover when to diagram, abbreviations, speed, checking meaning, and when writing both forms helps. Negative-room counterexample lab and four-combination table establish the single violation of a conditional. |
| 13 | **Put the whole process together** | **Dedicated instruction page:** identify indicator and full conditions, build original and contrapositive, read both, inspect/retry. **Exercise:** nine sentences, including qualification, clause order, only/only-if/the-only, requirement-first wording, and negative left/right/both conditions. Original and contrapositive choices must be checked before advancing; earlier choices remain mounted. |

The shared note explanations and embedded checks are in [ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx:207), with the expression explanations and labs in [ConditionalOpeningLesson.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalOpeningLesson.tsx:797). All four dedicated instruction-page implementations are in [OpeningCourse.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/OpeningCourse.tsx:43).

**The full recorded curriculum continues beyond that opening.** Its actual order comes from the generated runtime curriculum, rather than the declaration order of the authoring files.

| Phase | Ordered units and their substantive coverage |
|---|---|
| Foundations and straightforward translation | **Orientation**; **sufficient/necessary**; **Group 1**; **Group 2**; **rules versus facts**; **truth versus validity**; **simple negation**; **contraposition**. Covers the relationship, applying facts, true premises with false conclusions, exact predicate denial, and equivalent reverse-negated rules. |
| Remaining translation families | **Group 3:** unless, until, without, existing negatives and temporal boundaries. **Group 4:** exclusions, forbidden coexistence, without assuming exactly one or existence. **Mixed translation:** select among all four procedures. **Implicit conditionals:** guarantees, definitions and requirements without a familiar indicator. |
| Linking and inference | **Direct linking:** exact result-to-trigger chains and new rules versus case conclusions. **No-link:** shared triggers/results and mismatched subjects/qualifiers. **Triggering:** use established facts or missing requirements, without assuming a trigger. |
| Compound and scoped logic | **AND/OR:** joint versus alternative conditions. **De Morgan:** compound negation and contraposition. **Domain:** population, time and predicate restrictions. **Biconditionals:** both directions, separately recorded. **Whole-rule negation:** trigger true/result false counterexample, distinguished from contraposition. |
| Logical Reasoning application | **Must Be True**; **sufficient assumption**; **necessary assumption**; **flaw**; **parallel reasoning**; **principle**. Covers guaranteed conclusions, missing bridges, argument requirements and negation testing, invalid moves/counterexamples, structural matching, and application versus justification/illustration. |
| Quantifiers | **Meaning:** some/most/all/no, existence and denominators. **Negation:** exact denials and half cases. **Valid linking:** witnesses through universal rules and same-population majority overlap. **Invalid linking:** unsupported overlap, reversed majorities and invalid partial chains. |

Foundation/translation/linking authoring is in [foundations.source.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/content/foundations.source.ts:29); advanced logic, application and quantifiers are in [applications.source.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/content/applications.source.ts:27). [curriculumPath.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/curriculumPath.ts:4) specifies teaching-point difficulty and keeps quantifiers after conditional units.

For each recorded unit, the pattern is **lesson → guided example → skill drill → review/repair**. Later lessons include teaching paragraphs, a worked example, an interaction, a method and common-mistake repair. Guided/practice routes ask for written reasoning before choices, offer hints/explanations, check the choice and record the attempt. Unlike the four revised opening drills, they have introductory instructions on the exercise surface rather than a separate Start landing. See [ConditionalLessonNote.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalLessonNote.tsx:32) and [routes.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/routes.tsx:241).

Actual coverage limits:

- **The revised opening is not the whole bootcamp.** Group 3/4, chains, compounds, applications and quantifiers exist, but their pages have not been rebuilt into the new ordered note/drill shell.
- **There is a progression seam.** The last revised opening destination returns to Lessons. Visiting or finishing opening content does not mark recorded lesson completion. The recorded recommendation can therefore still point to the opening Lessons index; there is no automatic reviewed transition into the later curriculum. [routes.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/routes.tsx:222), [OpeningCourse.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/OpeningCourse.tsx:126).
- **Later practice banks are small:** most units have three questions per difficulty band. Group 1/2 have larger banks. This supplies coverage, not evidence of stable retention or extensive transfer.
- **Prerequisites describe the intended order; authorization gates enforce assignment scope.** Direct access is not a demonstrated-mastery gate.
- **Written reasoning is not automatically graded.** Checked choices, diagrams, corrections and lesson-read markers cannot establish independent mastery.
- External official-question sets and practice worlds are linked resources, not integrated proof that every later skill has been mastered. [content/index.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/content/index.ts:29).

The pen has not been dropped. | Separate a hypothetical rule from a fact that satisfies it. |\\r\\n| 1:48–2:15 | Sufficient means enough to establish the other condition. Necessary is what must hold when the sufficient condition holds. | Give each technical term an ordinary meaning and a stable example. |\\r\\n| 2:40–2:59 | Sufficient belongs left and necessary right in the arrow representation. | Introduce notation only after explaining the roles. |\\r\\n| 3:35–5:17 | If the pen did not fall, it could not have been dropped under the stated rule. Later reasoning is mainly a narrated contrapositive demonstration, not a supplied exercise bank. Do not claim the clip includes multiple-choice questions or a reviewed answer key.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How this belongs in Joshua\'s lesson\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [existing 13-part source map](../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) still controls progression. Use the [selected teaching voice](../../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md).\\r\\n\\r\\nOriginal adaptation: **If a display lamp is lit, its battery is installed.** First give only the rule and ask whether it establishes that the lamp is lit. Then add the fact that it is lit and ask what follows. Later, after explaining the necessary role, ask what follows if the battery is absent. Keep the same lamp and the same stated rule so the changing fact is the learner\'s focus.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is an authored hypothetical, not a technical claim about every real lamp. Introduce it explicitly as the rule for this exercise. Use fresh objects for independent practice after the walkthrough.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Boundaries and corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n- The source\'s phrasing that the rule is not “hard and fast” could suggest exceptions. Our conditional has no exception when its sufficient condition holds; what is conditional is its application to a case.\\r\\n- A trigger need not cause an event, and a conditional need not describe a time sequence. The arrow means implication under the stated rule.\\r\\n- Remove the source\'s weapon analogy and dismissive comparisons with schoolchildren. The entire supplied article and answer key were read on 2026-10-03.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Preserved evidence\\r\\n\\r\\n- [Exact clip](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-mastering-conditional-statements-2026-10-03/Mastering%20Conditional%20Statements.md), 10,036 bytes.\\r\\n- [Provenance](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-mastering-conditional-statements-2026-10-03/PROVENANCE.md) and [SHA-256 manifest](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-mastering-conditional-statements-2026-10-03/SHA256SUMS).\\r\\n- SHA-256: `814c346c022473d0f3ac362060969c2aec76a1fa5ec0a577466e2776ffec9061`.\\r\\n- Publisher attribution: LSAT Demon, supported by first-party links and signup invitation. Inbox last-write date was 2026-10-03; original retained unchanged.\\r\\n- No matching archived hash/source summary existed before this intake. No local images occur in the clip. Embedded YouTube links were not played, and the browser-extension iframe was not executed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What the article does\\r\\n\\r\\nThe article starts with ordinary conditional language and defines sufficient as enough to establish the other condition under the supplied rule. Its poison/sickness anchor demonstrates that a sufficient condition guarantees the necessary condition without making the reverse inference valid. It asks readers to accept a supplied premise rather than invent real-world exceptions.\\r\\n\\r\\nIts most useful teaching passage supplies a deliberately artificial restaurant-meal/tax-credit rule. It then asks what someone **needs** to do to receive the credit. The tempting answer mistakes a guaranteed route for the only route. Other routes could fit the rule. This distinguishes “enough for the result” from “required for the result” using an ordinary question rather than labels alone.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe article also demonstrates if-clauses at the end of sentences and omitted “then.” Its examples concern crops, a car-payment instruction and ability to sell spiders after cleaning cages. These are evidence of the article\'s method, not recommended student-facing examples.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The supplied six-question structure\\r\\n\\r\\nThe article uses a satirical law-firm/misery conditional. Abstract it as A → B for source analysis:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Question function | Supplied answer, paraphrased | Precise interpretation for adaptation |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| What is sufficient for B? | A. | A establishes B under the supplied rule. |\\r\\n| What is necessary for B? | Unknown. | The rule does not establish that A is required for B. Do not claim absolutely no necessary conditions exist. |\\r\\n| What is sufficient for A? | Unknown. | The rule does not establish that B is enough for A. Do not deny trivial or other independently supplied sufficient conditions. |\\r\\n| What is necessary for A? | B. | A cannot hold while B is false under the rule. |\\r\\n| Which clause is necessary for the other? | The then-clause. | B is required for A. |\\r\\n| Which clause needs the other? | The if-clause. | A needs B. This wording tests the learner\'s understanding from the opposite grammatical perspective. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThe distinction between the last two questions is particularly useful: **B is required for A** and **A requires B** describe the same relationship. Ask both naturally without turning the exercise into a vocabulary trick.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original adaptation authorized for development\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua approved an original raffle example modeled on this teaching pattern: **If you win this raffle, you get a bicycle.** The relationship is supplied for the exercise, not a claim about every raffle. Winning is enough to establish getting a bicycle. Getting a bicycle alone does not establish winning this raffle: receiving one as a gift or buying one could be consistent alternatives.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the alternatives as possible cases, not new premises about a particular person. Scope each question to what this rule establishes. “Does this rule make winning the raffle necessary for getting a bicycle?” is clearer than asking for an unrestricted inventory of every necessary condition for obtaining a bicycle.\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter the roles have been explained, vary the supplied fact and ask what follows, then ask the learner to describe a bicycle recipient who did not win the raffle. Later contraposition can ask whether someone who never gets a bicycle could satisfy the winning condition under this same rule. Avoid ambiguous snapshots such as “doesn\'t have the bicycle yet,” which do not deny eventual receipt. The [existing source map](../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) owns placement. The [selected teaching voice](../../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md) continues to govern prose.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis records an authorized example direction, not a claim that an app revision, assignment or publication has occurred.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Limits and corrections before reuse\\r\\n\\r\\n- Unsupported prevalence claims, scholarship/tax implications, medical assertions and the law-firm caricature are not imported into student material.\\r\\n- The article\'s statement that a then-clause is not sufficient and an if-clause is not necessary is too absolute. A supplied A → B does not establish B → A; another rule could establish it. Name the missing inference rather than declaring the roles impossible.\\r\\n- “Nothing can fill the blank” overstates what is unknown. Restrict the question to the relation between the two named conditions established by this rule.\\r\\n- Distinguish instructions and permission/ability from observed compliance. A car-payment instruction does not prove how someone paid; ability to sell does not prove a sale.\\r\\n- A premise accepted for an exercise need not be causal, chronological or independently plausible. Do not turn every conditional into a physical trigger.\\r\\n- The article supplies examples and teaching advice, not comparative learning-science evidence. Do not claim measured learning gains from adopting its question pattern.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: [Understanding Sufficient v. Necessary](lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary.md), [Abstract Conditionals](lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals.md). These are three distinct clipped sources.
