The entire supplied transcript, 0:00 to 9:10, was read. The closing fragments are incomplete. No source URL, speaker identity, local images or video embed are supplied. No unseen boards or missing speech were reconstructed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Preserved evidence\\r\\n\\r\\n- [Exact Markdown clip](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals-2026-10-03/LSAT%20Demon%20%20Abstract%20Conditionals.md), 6,712 bytes.\\r\\n- [Provenance](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals-2026-10-03/PROVENANCE.md) and [hash manifest](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals-2026-10-03/SHA256SUMS).\\r\\n- SHA-256: `89a4f5266dc577f09ea99de2a21b77c10d7887724d140e823a04c89b9e1129ee`.\\r\\n- Publication and capture dates unknown. Inbox last-write date was 2026-10-03. Archived and ingested 2026-10-03. Original retained unchanged; no matching archived hash or completed source summary found before intake.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What the transcript actually contains\\r\\n\\r\\n| Timestamp | Source content, paraphrased | Scope and use |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 0:44–1:37 | Boston implies Massachusetts. Not being in Boston does not settle whether a person is in Massachusetts. Not being in Massachusetts excludes Boston. | Compare absent sufficient with absent necessary. Use an original familiar relationship. |\\r\\n| 1:37–3:04 | A stipulated psychology/sociology rule can be accepted for the question even if real course registration works differently. The speaker offers several equivalent forms. | Teach students to reason from the supplied rule, without inventing an explanation for why it exists. |\\r\\n| 3:27–3:56 | Swap the conditions and negate both to form the contrapositive. | Reserve the symbolic operation until the concept and notation have been taught. |\\r\\n| 4:19–5:34 | Progress to X → ¬Y and its contrapositive Y → ¬X; paraphrase using only if and unless. | Negative conditions and abstract labels belong after the notation prerequisites. Unless stays in its later language lesson. |\\r\\n| 6:06–7:36 | Critique unsupported conclusions from ¬Y, then use a smoking/health analogy to make the reverse error concrete. | Keep the counterexample technique; replace the medical example and check both proposed conclusions. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are narrated prompts and demonstrations, not a formal supplied question set. The clip names student concerns about abstract rules. It does not provide a bank of standalone questions, choices or a reviewed answer key.\\r\\n\\r\\n## An explicit transcript discrepancy\\r\\n\\r\\nAt 6:06 the transcript criticizes deriving **¬X** from **¬Y** under **X → ¬Y**. At 6:34 it criticizes deriving **X** from **¬Y**. These are different proposed conclusions. Both are unsupported, but the transcript shifts between them. We cannot identify whether this was a speaker correction or transcription error without playback.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe logically correct teaching point is: given X → ¬Y and ¬Y, X could be true or false. Both X/¬Y and ¬X/¬Y satisfy the rule. Preserve the discrepancy as evidence; do not silently attribute a polished, consistent exercise to the source.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original adaptations for the bootcamp\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the [existing source map](../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) and [selected voice](../../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md). These are newly authored examples inspired by the teaching functions above, not source quotations or published assignments.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Familiar inclusion:** Every square is a rectangle. A shape is not a square. Can it still be a rectangle? Yes. A rectangle with unequal adjacent sides supplies a possible case. Use only if these shape meanings are clear; the logic must not turn into a geometry test.\\r\\n2. **Stipulated rule:** Every ticket in Drawer R has a blue border. A ticket is in Drawer R. What follows? It has a blue border. The exercise does not need to explain why tickets were sorted this way.\\r\\n3. **Wording comparison:** “Only blue-bordered tickets are in Drawer R” and “A ticket is in Drawer R only if it has a blue border” both express Drawer R → Blue border. Ask learners to choose the matching relationship and explain what the sentence requires.\\r\\n4. **Negative-condition transfer:** If a room is showing a film, it is not hosting a workshop. The room is not hosting a workshop. Does that settle whether a film is showing? No. Ask the learner to build two possible rooms: film/no workshop and no film/no workshop. Both fit. This directly demonstrates why the reverse inference fails.\\r\\n5. **Delayed abstract retrieval:** After the negative-condition lesson, show X → ¬Y and ask which fact rules out X. Y does, because X would require ¬Y. Ask separately what ¬Y establishes about X: nothing definite. Keep the two questions distinct.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Do not import these source habits\\r\\n\\r\\n- Saying a rule no longer matters when one trigger is absent. Keep it available for later facts and other inferences.\\r\\n- Profanity, ridicule or dismissive characterizations of a learner\'s reasoning.\\r\\n- Smoking as a universally sufficient condition for an undefined “not healthy.” That analogy introduces vague and contestable content unrelated to learning the inference.\\r\\n- Legacy Logic Games framing, source promotion or unsupported learning guarantees.\\r\\n- The source\'s hurried “the only”/“must” sentence as a clean indicator template. Use a grammatical original and preserve obligation versus compliance.\\r\\n- Unless/without before their transformations have been taught. Keep all topic prerequisites in the existing 13-part progression and later-unit boundaries.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: [sufficient/necessary clip](lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary.md), [LSAT Lab supplement](lsat-lab-conditional-logic-clip.md), [selected voice source](conditional-reasoning-voice.md).\\r\\n"}}}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 10.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Warning: truncated output (original token count: 12877)\nTotal output lines: 3\n\n{"i":0,"r":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"4b1859","wall_time_seconds":1.1349012,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":14207,"output":"Warning: truncated output (original token count: 14207)\\nTotal output lines: 628\\n\\n---\\r\\ntype: synthesis\\r\\nsubject: LSAT teaching voice standard\\r\\ncreated: 2026-10-02\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-03\\r\\naliases: [LSAT voice reference, Conditional transcription writing standard]\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, writing]\\r\\nsources:\\r\\n  - ../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# LSAT teaching: make the reasoning sound like someone thinking\\r\\n\\r\\n**This is Joshua\'s selected reference for writing LSAT teaching material.** Use it for bootcamp lessons, lecture notes, explanations, guided examples, drills, flashcards, quizzes, reference pages, and instructional feedback. It develops the teaching-content register in [the canonical teaching voice](../wiki/teaching-voice.md). That document still governs correspondence and marketing in their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua selected the supplied **Conditional Reasoning** transcription on 2026-10-02 because of its writing, tone, word choice, cadence, point of view, progression, and depth. The goal is to reproduce those qualities closely through original wording and examples. The central quality is patient, conversational reasoning that the reader can follow and eventually perform.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is a calibration example. This guide separates **observed features** from **instructions for our material**. A source habit is not automatically a rule, a research finding, or permission to import a topic. Matching the voice does not require repeating the same metaphors, anecdotes, exercise sentences, or personal claims.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Find the part you need\\r\\n\\r\\n- [The evidence and coverage](#the-evidence-and-coverage)\\r\\n- [The voice in one original passage](#the-voice-in-one-original-passage)\\r\\n- [How the teacher relates to the reader](#how-the-teacher-relates-to-the-reader)\\r\\n- [Sentence length and spoken cadence](#sentence-length-and-spoken-cadence)\\r\\n- [Word choice and useful verbal habits](#word-choice-and-useful-verbal-habits)\\r\\n- [Questions that make the reader think](#questions-that-make-the-reader-think)\\r\\n- [Transitions, repetition, metaphor, and emphasis](#transitions-explain-why-the-next-move-follows)\\r\\n- [The complete source progression and depth](#the-complete-source-progression-and-depth)\\r\\n- [What to carry into the Conditional Bootcamp](#what-to-carry-into-the-conditional-bootcamp)\\r\\n- [Accuracy and method boundaries](#accuracy-and-method-boundaries)\\r\\n- [Calibration examples and review](#calibration-examples-for-different-lsat-surfaces)\\r\\n- [A reusable writing brief](#a-reusable-writing-brief)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The evidence and coverage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [source summary](../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) identifies the [preserved HTML](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html), [provenance](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/PROVENANCE.md), and SHA-256. Every supplied section, FAQ entry, table, worked diagram, and drill item was read. HTML line references below refer to that unchanged archived file.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe document has six main sections and six subordinate headings. It ends with six basic drill items and an answer-key reference. One line is explicitly marked partially obscured. The answer key is not supplied. This analysis covers the entire attachment; it cannot reconstruct the missing line or establish the contents of the larger chapter.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe HTML says its formatting was adjusted. We can examine what a pause, table, side note, or separated example does for learning. We cannot claim its font, spacing, color, or CSS exactly reproduces the original publication. No author is identified in the file. The exercise wording attributed to Shakespeare is separate from the narrator\'s teaching voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The voice in one original passage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following is a new calibration passage. Its example was created for this guide; it is not a source quotation or an approved bootcamp page.\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose a shop has this rule: **Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You pick up a parcel with a blue sticker. What do you know about it?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> It has been inspected. The rule covers every parcel with that sticker, including the one in your hand. A blue-sticker parcel that hadn\'t been inspected would break the rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now turn the parcel over. It has an inspection stamp, but you can\'t see a blue sticker. Does it have to have one?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We don\'t know. The rule tells us something about parcels with blue stickers. It doesn\'t tell us that every inspected parcel gets a sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That\'s the distinction we need: **what the sentence makes certain, and what it leaves open.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice the opening definition before the example, the small prediction, the explanation connecting the rule to the case, and the change in what the reader is given. The last sentence names a distinction the reader has just seen. The passage has a conversational rhythm because it follows a person\'s thoughts. Casual vocabulary alone would not accomplish that.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn an interactive lesson, pause after the first question and again after the inspection-stamp question. Reveal each explanation after the learner has had an opportunity to answer. The printed passage shows the whole progression for calibration.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How the teacher relates to the reader\\r\\n\\r\\n### The reader is beside the teacher\\r\\n\\r\\nThe narrator talks directly to someone doing the work. “Let\'s,” “you,” and “we” keep the reader involved. The writing seldom steps back to describe what students generally do. It asks this reader to notice, try, decide, or check something now.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe reader is treated as capable of understanding ordinary meaning. The teacher supplies support when a technical step is new. In the opening, the source first gives the literal relationship, then asks the reader to take its certainty seriously. Later, it encourages a guess before revealing the contrapositive. These are expectations of participation, not claims that everything should feel easy.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** speak to the reader without making their intelligence the subject. Do not copy a line such as “Because you\'re a thinking human.” Give them a manageable question and the information to answer it. If they miss it, explain the precise move that went wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Confidence lives in the reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is decisive about a valid consequence. It also says “We don\'t know” when the information cannot settle a question. These two kinds of confidence belong together. ## assistant

Use this definition **before** the existing law-school example:

> **Sufficient means enough.** A sufficient condition gives you enough information to know that another condition is true. Once you know the sufficient condition is true, the other condition must be true too. You don't need another fact to establish it.
>
> That's what **guarantee** means here: the sufficient condition cannot be true while the other condition is false.

Then retain:

> If you're enrolled in law school, you're a student.
>
> Knowing you're enrolled in law school is enough to know you're a student. You don't need to know which law school you attend or which classes you're taking.

Replace the cause aside with:

> **Enough does not mean the only way**
>
> Being enrolled in law school is enough to know you're a student. That doesn't make law-school enrollment the only way to be a student.
>
> If you aren't enrolled in law school, you could still be a student. Not meeting a sufficient condition does not, by itself, rule out the other condition.

This teaches three distinctions: **enough information → certainty → other possibilities remain open**. It avoids making the definition depend on wording or introducing a separate causality topic.

Source support:

- [LSAT Lab transcript, 00:33–01:04](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/16784/source.en-US.vtt:52): sufficient condition true requires the other condition true. At 01:14–01:43, an absent sufficient condition leaves the other unsettled.
- [Demon sufficient/necessary, 01:48–02:15](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary.md:29): sufficient means enough.
- [Demon mastering conditionals](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-mastering-conditional-statements.md:28): a sufficient route need not be the only route.
- [Demon abstract conditionals, 00:44–01:37](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals.md:27): absence of the sufficient condition leaves both possibilities open.
- [Joshua’s corrections](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md:31): explain guarantee and sufficient in ordinary language before relying on them.

No edits made.

If I’m breathing, there’s air around. The core of the relationship is that simple. If we have one thing, we <strong>must</strong> have the other thing. Just like with the Power Players, we have to take this <strong>MUST</strong> seriously. There is no way around this relationship. If you have the first thing, you have to have the second thing.</p>\\r\\n152:<p>For all the ballyhoo about conditional reasoning, you would think it’s a lot more complicated than that. The key to keeping conditional reasoning simple through its many applications, which we will examine in detail throughout this chapter, is understanding the concept behind it. I want you to intuitively understand the relationship at the heart of conditionals. Once you have that, the verbal idiosyncrasies that separate one conditional from another will be nothing more than blips on the radar.</p>\\r\\n154:<p>Let’s start by taking our conditional example apart piece by piece.</p>\\r\\n156:<h3>The Sufficient Condition</h3>\\r\\n158:<div class=\\"callout\\">The “if” part of the conditional is called the sufficient condition.</div>\\r\\n160:<p class=\\"example\\">If I’m breathing, then air is present.</p>\\r\\n162:<p>The sufficient condition is a door opener. It’s welcoming. It could occur, but it doesn’t have to. Just like an open door, someone may walk in, but they don’t have to. In the example, I might be breathing or I might not: I could be holding my breath trying to get rid of hiccups or I could be breathing. We don’t know. We just know what will happen if I <em>am</em> breathing.</p>\\r\\n164:<p><strong>If the sufficient condition is absent, you can completely ignore the conditional statement.</strong> If I’m not breathing, this conditional doesn’t matter at all. There might be air; there might not be air. The conditional wasn’t activated, so who cares? I’m not breathing, so it doesn’t matter.</p>\\r\\n166:<p><strong>But if the sufficient condition is present, the conditional statement must be followed.</strong> If I am breathing, there absolutely 100% has to be air. The conditional statement gets activated and everything goes according to plan.</p>\\r\\n169:  <strong>What does it mean to activate a conditional?</strong>\\r\\n170:  <p>It means the sufficient condition is present! So the conditional must be followed.</p>\\r\\n173:<p>The sufficient condition extends beyond just the word “if.” There is a whole family of words that work just like “if”; they let you know you have a sufficient condition on your hands.</p>\\r\\n175:<p>Here are the members of the sufficient family:</p>\\r\\n178:  <thead><tr><th>Sufficient Indicators</th><th>Example</th></tr></thead>\\r\\n180:    <tr><td>if</td><td><em>If I’m breathing, then air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n181:    <tr><td>when(ever)</td><td><em>When I’m breathing, air is present.</em><br><br><em>Whenever I’m breathing, air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n182:    <tr><td>any(time)</td><td><em>Any breathing requires that air is present.</em><br><br><em>Anytime I’m breathing, air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n183:    <tr><td>all</td><td><em>All instances of breathing have air present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n184:    <tr><td>every(time)</td><td><em>Every instance of breathing has air present.</em><br><br><em>Everytime I’m breathing, air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n187:    <tr><td>each</td><td><em>Each instance of breathing has air.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n191:<p>Notice how all of the sufficient family members have similar personalities. They are all inclusive, open words. Think back to the similarities between these words if/when you get lost in complex language.</p>\\r\\n193:<p>I had to smooth out some of the linguistic rough edges to translate that conditional into all the different versions, but the core relationship remained the same. <strong>Language is the challenge of conditionals; you have to distill the same conditional relationship from many different wording combinations.</strong> This is why it’s so important to understand the relationship on a deeper level than “look for indicator words.” The words are the hard part, so relying on indicators exclusively is a ticking time bomb.</p>\\r\\n197:  <p>The parentheses are referring to an optional addition to the original word. Both “when” and “whenever” are members of the sufficient family. Conditionally, all of the examples in the chart above mean exactly the same thing as our initial example.</p>\\r\\n202:<div class=\\"callout\\">The “then” part of the conditional is called the necessary condition.</div>\\r\\n204:<p class=\\"example\\">If I’m breathing, then air is present.</p>\\r\\n206:<p>The necessary condition slams the door that the sufficient condition opens. It is the place of certainty. I mean just look at its name! It’s called the <em>necessary</em> condition because it is literally necessary. It has to occur at some point if the conditional relationship is activated. You can prove things that live in the necessary condition.</p>\\r\\n208:<p>There is a family of words that serves the same purpose as “then.” Each of these words lets you know you have a necessary condition in play. Here are the members of the necessary family:</p>\\r\\n213:    <tr><td>then</td><td><em>If I’m breathing, then air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n"}'}]

## assistant

The current lesson is **more explicit than the original about what “enough” means**, but repetition still outweighs the missing distinction.

What it does well:

- Defines sufficient before the example and explains guarantee as certainty. [ReferenceSequence:224](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx:224).
- Uses one stable law-school relationship through explanation, interaction and group diagram.
- Shows the forbidden combination: enrolled, but not a student. It also shows that students outside law school are allowed. [Experience:4](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/SufficientConditionExperience.tsx:4).
- Avoids the original’s misleading claim that an absent sufficient condition lets you ignore the rule entirely. [Original HTML:164](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html:164).

Remaining gaps:

1. **Explain the condition before asking whether it holds.** The page identifies enrollment correctly, but never plainly separates “being enrolled” as a condition from knowing that someone actually is enrolled. The original supplies that uncertainty before contrasting presence and absence. [Original:162](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html:162).

2. **The absent-condition explanation is incomplete.** “A student outside law school” establishes one allowed possibility. It does not explicitly show that someone outside law school could be a student **or not be a student**. That second possibility completes the distinction: enrollment establishes student status; absence of enrollment leaves it unsettled. [Experience:18](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/SufficientConditionExperience.tsx:18). LSAT Lab makes this contrast at 01:14–01:43; [Demon’s abstract source](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals.md:27) does likewise.

3. **Several sections repeat instead of advance.** Opening paragraphs, example explanation, walkthrough selections, default group diagram and later aside repeatedly establish enrollment → student. The grades/classes aside repeats the opening’s lack of extra requirements; graduation/lawyer claims add a scope boundary without developing sufficiency. [ReferenceSequence:225](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx:225), [aside:240](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx:240).

4. **The walkthrough returns to sentence anatomy too soon.** Its sufficient explanation starts with the word “if.” Here, explaining what enrollment guarantees would serve the concept better; indicator recognition belongs later. [Experience:90](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/SufficientConditionExperience.tsx:90).

5. **Both final checks chiefly test reversal.** Medical-school wording and the law-school requirement question cover similar inference errors. One check of what absent enrollment leaves open would broaden the assessment without introducing another example. [ReferenceSequence:246](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx:246).

Recommended progression: **enough for what → enrollment as the condition → enrollment present establishes student → enrollment absent leaves student status open → compare the permitted and forbidden combinations → check understanding**.

That follows the sources’ reasoning while keeping the existing example and avoiding their metaphors, ridicule and overstatements. No edits made.

## assistant

The whole sufficient page is **Reference section 2 plus the walkthrough and group explorer**. The opening-course wrapper adds no teaching content; it removes only the final transition. [OpeningCourseContent:260](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/OpeningCourseContent.tsx:260).

Recommended complete flow:

1. **Define enough before the example.** Explain that one condition ensures another holds, and that “guarantees” means certainty. Avoid defining the term by repeating it.
2. **Unpack law-school enrollment.** Enrollment is the condition; being a student is what it guarantees. No further requirement is needed.
3. **Explain its presence and absence.** Enrollment requires student status. Without enrollment, someone could be a student or not be a student. This distinction belongs before the interactive picture.
4. **Explore possible combinations.** Show enrolled/student, forbidden enrolled/not-student, and both possibilities outside enrollment. Clarify that these illustrate what the relationship permits.
5. **Ask two distinct questions.**
6. **Bridge briefly to necessary.** Being a student must hold whenever enrollment holds; the next lesson explains that required role.

Precise cuts and consolidation:

- Combine the opening three paragraphs into one definition and one explanation of certainty. [ReferenceSequence:224](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx:224).
- Remove the standalone trigger paragraph. It introduces another name without developing the concept.
- Remove the grades/classes/graduation/lawyer aside. It repeats the initial explanation and opens a different scope question. [ReferenceSequence:239](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx:239).
- Remove “if” recognition from the walkthrough’s condition explanation. Explain enrollment itself here; teach indicator vocabulary later. [Experience:90](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/SufficientConditionExperience.tsx:90).
- Keep both visual components only if their jobs differ: the walkthrough reveals what enrollment guarantees; the group explorer tests permitted and forbidden combinations. Their explanations should not repeat the same guarantee.

Two distinct checks:

**Which combination would break this relationship?**

- Enrolled in law school and a student.
- **Enrolled in law school, but not a student.**
- A student who is not enrolled in law school.

Correct explanation: “Enrollment guarantees being a student. Someone enrolled who wasn't a student would contradict that guarantee.”

**You're not enrolled in law school. What does that tell us about whether you're a student?**

- You cannot be a student.
- You must be a student.
- **You could be a student or not be a student.**

Correct explanation: “Enrollment would establish that you're a student. Without enrollment, this relationship leaves your student status open.”

This retains the intuitive example and covers certainty, the condition’s identity, presence, absence and the limit of the guarantee without introducing another topic. No edits made.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 13.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"d68790","wall_time_seconds":0.3908677,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3340,"output":"---\\r\\ntitle: Teaching Voice\\r\\ntype: concept\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, content]\\r\\ncreated: 2026-06-10\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-02\\r\\nstatus: active\\r\\nsubject: Teaching Voice\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Teaching Voice\\r\\n\\r\\nHow LSAT U sounds, across every surface. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n**LSAT teaching standard, selected 2026-10-02:** Joshua chose the supplied Conditional Reasoning transcription as the reference for how LSAT material should sound and unfold. Read [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md) before drafting lessons, notes, explanations, drills, flashcards, quizzes, or instructional feedback. It contains the detailed source analysis, original calibration examples, progression, and review rubric. [Source identity and limits](sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) are preserved separately. This choice develops the teaching-content register below; correspondence and marketing retain their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Air between ideas. Real correspondence is short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters). In teaching, vary sentence and paragraph length with the reasoning: give an explanation room, then let a short sentence settle the consequence. Do not impose email brevity on a lesson or cut its intermediate reasoning.\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\"; \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs: never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, personal encouragement, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (conversational reasoning) -- lessons, recaps, notes, drills, explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nUse [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md), Joshua\'s selected calibration from 2026-10-02. Keep the reader beside the teacher. Explain the ordinary meaning, ground it in an original example, make the small inferences audible, ask a useful question, and show both the consequence and its limit. Introduce terminology and notation when their meaning is established. Give each concept enough development to be learned from the page.\\r\\n\\r\\nContractions and varied sentence lengths should sound natural when read aloud. Repetition should change the reader\'s view of the same relationship. Questions should give the reader actual thinking work. Light humor may appear within an explanation when it helps understanding; this supersedes the older wit-only-at-the-edges restriction. Do not force punchlines, slang, hyperbole, catchphrases, or paragraph quotas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source governs delivery, not Joshua\'s procedure, indicator taxonomy, biography, or the scope of a lesson. Preserve his approved methods and logical precision. Personal encouragement still follows the earnest coaching register. Project-owned `lsat-u-voice` routes here and to the detailed standard; an older vendor writer-blend skill must not override this selection.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed \\"the next card is the page in front of you\\" was clever but empty).\\r\\n\\r\\n> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrand copy speaks as the platform (\\"we\\", \\"you\\"), not as an individual (\\"I\\", \\"Joshua\\"). (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)\\r\\n- No condescension or empty cheerleading. ## assistant

For the indicator list:

> You won't always see **if**. Other words and phrases can also help you recognize a sufficient condition:
>
> [Existing list]
>
> These are clues to the relationship. Ask what one condition guarantees, rather than stopping when you spot a familiar word.

“Words and phrases” names what the learner sees. Preserve the existing list, but avoid implying that every listed word automatically makes the following words sufficient. The original table explains them through complete conditional relationships. [Original HTML:173](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html:173).

Give the ending a deliberate purpose:

> Let's check what enrollment establishes, and what its absence leaves open.

**Question 1:** “You're enrolled in law school. Under this relationship, must you be a student?”

- **Yes. Enrollment guarantees it.**
- No. Enrollment only makes it likely.

Feedback: “Enrollment is enough to establish that you're a student. Someone enrolled who wasn't a student would break the relationship.”

**Question 2:** “You aren't enrolled in law school. What can we conclude about whether you're a student?”

- You cannot be a student.
- **You could be a student or not be a student.**

Feedback: “Enrollment would establish that you're a student. Without enrollment, both possibilities remain open.”

The first checks **certainty when the condition holds**. The second checks **uncertainty when it does not**. Replacing law school with medical school repeats the same relationship without adding a distinct thinking task.

No edits made.

There are no local image references to inspect.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Preserved evidence\\r\\n\\r\\n- [Exact Markdown clip](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary-2026-10-03/LSAT%20Demon%20%20Understanding%20Sufficient%20v.%20Necessary.md), 3,854 bytes.\\r\\n- [Provenance](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary-2026-10-03/PROVENANCE.md) and [hash manifest](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary-2026-10-03/SHA256SUMS).\\r\\n- SHA-256: `1fa38af6382cbc3f77efe9785499ef5416f0c4eabfcc074370a7bb6c05ebdb7f`.\\r\\n- Publication and capture dates unknown. Original retained unchanged; no matching archived hash or completed source summary found before intake.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What the source teaches\\r\\n\\r\\n| Timestamp | Source content, paraphrased | Useful teaching function |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 0:04–0:26 | A conditional is a rule qualified by a condition, and several phrasings may state the same relationship. | Define the relationship before teaching vocabulary. |\\r\\n| 0:51–1:31 | The speaker says a dropped pen will fall, then asks whether that establishes it will fall for sure. The pen has not been dropped. | Separate a hypothetical rule from a fact that satisfies it. |\\r\\n| 1:48–2:15 | Sufficient means enough to establish the other condition. Necessary is what must hold when the sufficient condition holds. | Give each technical term an ordinary meaning and a stable example. |\\r\\n| 2:40–2:59 | Sufficient belongs left and necessary right in the arrow representation. | Introduce notation only after explaining the roles. |\\r\\n| 3:35–5:17 | If the pen did not fall, it could not have been dropped under the stated rule. The source calls this the contrapositive and emphasizes equivalence. | Ask for the consequence of a missing requirement before naming the operation. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThe only explicit opening question asks whether the rule itself establishes that the pen will fall. Later reasoning is mainly a narrated contrapositive demonstration, not a supplied exercise bank. Do not claim the clip includes multiple-choice questions or a reviewed answer key.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How this belongs in Joshua\'s lesson\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [existing 13-part source map](../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) still controls progression. This source supports deeper examples in the rule/fact, sufficient, necessary and conceptual-contrapositive sections. It does not replace the skeleton or Joshua\'s five construction steps. Use the [selected teaching voice](../../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md).\\r\\n\\r\\nOriginal adaptation: **If a display lamp is lit, its battery is installed.** First give only the rule and ask whether it establishes that the lamp is lit. Then add the fact that it is lit and ask what follows. Later, after explaining the necessary role, ask what follows if the battery is absent. Keep the same lamp and the same stated rule so the changing fact is the learner\'s focus.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is an authored hypothetical, not a technical claim about every real lamp. Introduce it explicitly as the rule for this exercise. Use fresh objects for independent practice after the walkthrough.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Boundaries and corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n- The source\'s phrasing that the rule is not “hard and fast” could suggest exceptions. Our conditional has no exception when its sufficient condition holds; what is conditional is its application to a case.\\r\\n- A trigger need not cause an event, and a conditional need not describe a time sequence. The arrow means implication under the stated rule.\\r\\n- Remove the source\'s weapon analogy and dismissive comparisons with schoolchildren. A learner\'s uncertainty deserves an explanation.\\r\\n- The missing sufficient condition does not remove the rule. It leaves the other condition unsettled by that fact and rule alone.\\r\\n- The clip is evidence of a teaching approach, not comparative learning-science evidence or proof of student outcomes.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: [abstract-conditionals continuation](lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals.md), [LSAT Lab supplement](lsat-lab-conditional-logic-clip.md), [selected voice Identify the two main concepts (groups, c\\ncorpus/Curriculum/Conditional Logic/Notes/_megadoc_notes_conditionals.md:62:Conditional logic forms the bedrock of many arguments and inferences tested on the LSAT requiring test-takers to demonstrate proficiency in recognizing the contrapositive logic and avoiding common illegal moves. While the provided sources do not detail every single LSAT Logical Reasoning question type (such as Parallel Reasoning or Method of Reasoning) they offer a comprehensive breakdown of the core activities required for analysis and specifically target the most critical error tested in Flaw questions. The breakdown of conditional logic primarily revolves around two main analytical activities: Chaining (deriving new rules) and Triggering (deriving new facts). I. General Breakdown Activity: Chaining Conditionals (Deriving New Rules). Chaining involves synthesizing multiple conditional rules to create a new inferred conditional statement. This is crucial for questions that require you to draw broad conclusions from a set of premises (often seen in Inference/Must Be True contexts). Connecting Rules: You must determine if the necessary condition (right side) of one conditional statement matches the sufficient condition (left side) of another. For instance if A rightarrow B and B rightarrow C they chain to infer a new conditional relationship: A rightarrow C. Contraposing Chains: You can contraposit an entire chain starting from the final necessary condition and negating back to the initial sufficient condition. If the chain is A rightarrow D the contrapositive is If not D then not A. The LSAT commonly rewards the ability to connect the beginning of the chain to the ending of the chain. Negating Complex Ideas: If the idea being contraposed (the trigger or the outcome) is a complex idea connected by and or or (e.g. A and B) you must remember to flip the truth values when negating. And turns into or and or turns into and. This ensures you correctly flip the truth value of everything in the complex idea. II. General Breakdown Activity: Triggering Conditionals (Deriving New Facts). Triggering is the process of using a known fact to activate a conditional rule and derive a certain factual inference. This is the process utilized in many Must Be True and Inference questions. A conditional rule (Sufficient rightarrow Necessary) can only be used in two valid scenarios: 1. Affirming the Sufficient Condition: If a fact confirms that the sufficient condition (the left side the trigger) is true then the necessary condition (the right side the outcome) must necessarily follow. 2. Denying the Necessary Condition (Contrapositive Logic): If a fact confirms that the necessary condition (the right side the outcome) is not true then the sufficient condition (the left side the trigger) cannot have been true. If the fact relates to the conditional rule in any other way (e.g. affirming the necessary or denying the sufficient) the rule just disappears and has no power over us. III. Breakdown in Specific Question Types and Contexts. Flaw Questions. Flaw questions are specifically designed to test whether you can recognize errors in conditional reasoning. The Conditional Flaw: The specific mistake frequently made by LSAT authors is confusing the necessary and the sufficient. This happens when an argument presents a rule (A rightarrow B) observes that the right side (the necessary condition B) is happening and then attempts to conclude that this proves the left side (the sufficient condition A) is happening. Breakdown Method: Your breakdown must identify the conditional rule and then recognize that the author has committed the illegal move of reading the conditional backward. This is the primary error the LSAT tries to ensure students avoid. For example learning that Alice is in the USA (necessary condition) does not allow you to conclude she is in NYC (sufficient condition). Inference and Must Be True Questions. These questions rely heavily on the ability to correctly apply the chaining and triggering activities described above. Breakdown Method: When presented with premises (rules) and facts you must diagram the conditionals and perform valid inferences. You must look for ways to chain rules together to find a connection from the premises to the answer choices.\\ncorpus/Curriculum/Conditional Logic/Notes/_megadoc_notes_conditionals.md:70:Figuring Out The Language. The What Test is designed to resolve ambiguities in sentences with conditional indicators by pinpointing exactly what the indicator refers to. How to Perform the What Test. This test involves adding a what to whichever side of the indicator makes grammatical sense helping clarify the target of the condition. If what? People who what? Depends on what? When what? Each what? Need what? Any what? Must what? Have to what? All what? Whats necessary? Whats essential? Every what? Whats required? Whats the precondition? In order to what? Only (if) what? This test is typically unnecessary for straightforward indicators like if and all but proves invaluable for more confusing indicators such as depends and required. Example of The What Test. Sentence: Air is required for breathing. Implementation: Question: What is required in this sentence? Answer: Air is the thing that is required. Personalized If/Then Strategy. Personalized If/Then is a technique used to translate conditional statements into personal contexts simplifying understanding and ensuring correct logical diagramming. How to Create a Personalized If/Then. 1. Understand the casual non-conditional meaning of the sentence. 2. Take a guess at which half of the statement is the sufficient condition. 3. Put yourself in the situation of your guess and ask what you know about yourself. 4. If your guess is correct you will find that the necessary condition has to pertain. Example Translation into Personalized If/Then. Original Statement: Orchids depend on frequent conversation. Casual Meaning: Orchids need frequent conversation. Guess: Orchids as the sufficient condition. Personalization: If Im an orchid what do I know about me? I depend on frequent conversation. If Im an orchid then I have frequent conversation. This method not only aids in understanding the conditional but also verifies its correctness. Incorrect guesses can be easily identified and corrected through this personal context. Advantages of Personalized If/Then. Helps intuitively understand conditionals by imagining yourself as part of the scenario. Provides confidence throughout tests especially in correctly interpreting conditionals not phrased as if/then statements. Both the What Test and Personalized If/Then Strategy are crucial tools in deciphering and applying conditional logic particularly in competitive exams like the LSAT.\\ncorpus/Curriculum/Conditional Logic/Notes/_megadoc_notes_conditionals.md:182:Word Bank. 1 none without. 100 some until. present or and. 51 absent nor. These are evidence of the article\'s method, not recommended student-facing examples.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The supplied six-question structure\\r\\n\\r\\nThe article uses a satirical law-firm/misery conditional. Abstract it as A → B for source analysis:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Question function | Supplied answer, paraphrased | Precise interpretation for adaptation |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| What is sufficient for B? | A. | A establishes B under the supplied rule. |\\r\\n| What is necessary for B? | Unknown. | The rule does not establish that A is required for B. Do not claim absolutely no necessary conditions exist. |\\r\\n| What is sufficient for A? | Unknown. | The rule does not establish that B is enough for A. Do not deny trivial or other independently supplied sufficient conditions. |\\r\\n| What is necessary for A? | B. | A cannot hold while B is false under the rule. |\\r\\n| Which clause is necessary for the other? | The then-clause. | B is required for A. |\\r\\n| Which clause needs the other? | The if-clause. | A needs B. This wording tests the learner\'s understanding from the opposite grammatical perspective. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThe distinction between the last two questions is particularly useful: **B is required for A** and **A requires B** describe the same relationship. Ask both naturally without turning the exercise into a vocabulary trick.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original adaptation authorized for development\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua approved an original raffle example modeled on this teaching pattern: **If you win this raffle, you get a bicycle.** The relationship is supplied for the exercise, not a claim about every raffle. Winning is enough to establish getting a bicycle. Getting a bicycle alone does not establish winning this raffle: receiving one as a gift or buying one could be consistent alternatives.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the alternatives as possible cases, not new premises about a particular person. Scope each question to what this rule establishes. “Does this rule make winning the raffle necessary for getting a bicycle?” is clearer than asking for an unrestricted inventory of every necessary condition for obtaining a bicycle.\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter the roles have been explained, vary the supplied fact and ask what follows, then ask the learner to describe a bicycle recipient who did not win the raffle. Later contraposition can ask whether someone who never gets a bicycle could satisfy the winning condition under this same rule. Avoid ambiguous snapshots such as “doesn\'t have the bicycle yet,” which do not deny eventual receipt. The [existing source map](../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) owns placement. The [selected teaching voice](../../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md) continues to govern prose.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis records an authorized example direction, not a claim that an app revision, assignment or publication has occurred.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Limits and corrections before reuse\\r\\n\\r\\n- Unsupported prevalence claims, scholarship/tax implications, medical assertions and the law-firm caricature are not imported into student material.\\r\\n- The article\'s statement that a then-clause is not sufficient and an if-clause is not necessary is too absolute. A supplied A → B does not establish B → A; another rule could establish it. Name the missing inference rather than declaring the roles impossible.\\r\\n- “Nothing can fill the blank” overstates what is unknown. Restrict the question to the relation between the two named conditions established by this rule.\\r\\n- Distinguish instructions and permission/ability from observed compliance. A car-payment instruction does not prove how someone paid; ability to sell does not prove a sale.\\r\\n- A premise accepted for an exercise need not be causal, chronological or independently plausible. Do not turn every conditional into a physical trigger.\\r\\n- The article supplies examples and teaching advice, not comparative learning-science evidence. Do not claim measured learning gains from adopting its question pattern.\\r\\n"}'}]

It is the place of certainty. I mean just look at its name! It’s called the <em>necessary</em> condition because it is literally necessary. It has to occur at some point if the conditional relationship is activated. You can prove things that live in the necessary condition.</p>\\n208:<p>There is a family of words that serves the same purpose as “then.” Each of these words lets you know you have a necessary condition in play. Here are the members of the necessary family:</p>\\n216:    <tr><td>required</td><td><em>Air is required for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\n236:<p>So far, we’ve explored the sufficient condition, the necessary condition, and the relationship between the two. Specifically, we’ve gone over the core of the conditional relationship:</p>\\n238:<p class=\\"example\\">If the sufficient condition occurs, then the necessary condition must occur.</p>\\n259:<p class=\\"example\\">If the necessary condition is absent, the sufficient condition is absent too. This is the contrapositive.</p>\\n267:<p>OK, so if I’m breathing, air is needed. I have to have air for the breathing to happen. The air is completely necessary. What if I don’t have air? That means I don’t have the thing I need. That implies that I couldn’t have activated my conditional relationship. So, I can’t be breathing. No necessary conditions means there’s no sufficient condition.</p>\\n269:<p><strong>The original statement and its contrapositive are all you know from your conditional relationship.</strong> The LSAT will try to tempt you into erroneously surmising other things from your conditional. Don’t fall for these ploys. For example, they will give you a conditional statement, and then say, “We know the necessary condition is happening!” When they do this, you should be like, “Cool. So I can ignore the conditional.” <strong>The presence of the necessary condition doesn’t make anything happen.</strong></p>\\n278:    <tr><td><strong>Sufficient Present</strong></td><td><em>Must have necessary condition</em></td><td><em>I’m breathing, so there must be air.</em></td></tr>\\n310:        required<br>\\n358:<p>There you go. Your first fully diagrammed conditional! Now let’s talk through the contrapositive. If the necessary condition is gone, we know the sufficient is gone as well. We can diagram the contrapositive as:</p>\\n461:    <tr><td><em>[Air] is required for breathing.</em></td><td></td></tr>\\n469:<p class=\\"example\\">[Air] is required for breathing. / I require [air] to breathe.</p>\\n491:  <li>If your guess is right, you will know that the necessary condition has to pertain.</li>\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 4.2 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"1ec2be","wall_time_seconds":0.3392528,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1008,"output":"198: </div>\\r\\n199: \\r\\n200: <h3>The Necessary Condition</h3>\\r\\n201: \\r\\n202: <div class=\\"callout\\">The “then” part of the conditional is called the necessary condition.</div>\\r\\n203: \\r\\n204: <p class=\\"example\\">If I’m breathing, then air is present.</p>\\r\\n205: \\r\\n206: <p>The necessary condition slams the door that the sufficient condition opens. It is the place of certainty. I mean just look at its name! It’s called the <em>necessary</em> condition because it is literally necessary. It has to occur at some point if the conditional relationship is activated. You can prove things that live in the necessary condition.</p>\\r\\n207: \\r\\n208: <p>There is a family of words that serves the same purpose as “then.” Each of these words lets you know you have a necessary condition in play. Here are the members of the necessary family:</p>\\r\\n209: \\r\\n210: <table>\\r\\n211:   <thead><tr><th>Necessary Indicators</th><th>Example</th></tr></thead>\\r\\n212:   <tbody>\\r\\n213:     <tr><td>then</td><td><em>If I’m breathing, then air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n214:     <tr><td>must</td><td><em>Air must be present for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n215:     <tr><td>necessary</td><td><em>Air is necessary for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n216:     <tr><td>required</td><td><em>Air is required for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n217:     <tr><td>only (if)</td><td><em>Only the presence of air allows for breathing.</em><br><br><em>I’m breathing, only if air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n218:     <tr><td>depends</td><td><em>Breathing depends on air being present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n219:     <tr><td>need (to)</td><td><em>I need air to breathe.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n220:     <tr><td>have to</td><td><em>I have to have air, if I’m breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n221:     <tr><td>essential</td><td><em>Air is essential for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n222:     <tr><td>precondition</td><td><em>Air is a precondition for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n223:   </tbody>\\r\\n224: </table>\\r\\n225: \\r\\n226: <p>Notice the similarities in each of these words. They are all ironclad words. They are serious and restrictive; they are obligations.</p>\\r\\n227: \\r\\n228: <p>All of those statements in the example column mean the exact same thing as the sufficient family examples. It is the exact same concept expressed in a bunch of different ways. What’s important isn’t how the conditional is expressed, but the core relationship hiding underneath the language. This is why we have a symbolic way of representing conditional relationships, to push past the language and focus only on the relationship between the two variables.</p>\\r\\n229: \\r\\n230: <div class=\\"note\\"><strong>Pay special attention to ONLY IF!</strong> It is a necessary indicator, even though it contains the word IF. You can think of it like the ONLY is dominant over a recessive IF.</div>\\r\\n231: \\r\\n232: <hr class=\\"page-break\\">\\r\\n7: Group 2: Basic Translation - Group 2\\r\\n8: GROUP 2: ONLY, ONLY IF, ONLY WHEN, ONLY WHERE, ALWAYS, MUST\\r\\n9: All the words in this group follow this translation rule:\\r\\n10: The ideas introduced by (i.e., immediately following) these words are the \\r\\n11: necessary conditions.\\r\\n12: Let’s Try It:\\r\\n13: Example Statement:\\r\\n14: \\"There will be an accomplishment of lasting value only if there is hard work.\\"\\r\\n15: Step 1: Identify the logical operator.\\r\\n16: Here, it’s “only if.”\\r\\n17: Step 2: Identify the two main concepts (or groups, categories, events, or \\r\\n18: ideas).\\r\\n19: Here, it’s the two events “accomplishment of lasting value” and “there is \\r\\n20: hard work.”\\r\\n21: Step 3: Assign symbols to the two main concepts.\\r\\n22: Here, “ALV” for “accomplishment of lasting value” and “HW” for “there is \\r\\n23: hard work.”\\r\\n24: Step 4: Apply the translation rule.\\r\\n25: The ideas introduced by these words are the necessary conditions.\\r\\n26: ALV → HW\\r\\n27: Step 5: Find the contrapositive.\\r\\n28: /HW → /ALV\\r\\n29: Step 6: Translate back to English.\\r\\n30: If there is no hard work, then there is not an accomplishment of lasting \\r\\n31: value.\\r\\n32: 1\\r\\n33: •\\r\\n34: •\\r\\n35: Explanation:\\r\\n"}'}]

Local sources agree on the core explanation:

> A necessary condition is something required for something else. If that requirement is missing, the thing that needs it cannot hold. Having the requirement, however, does not by itself establish that other thing.

The last sentence needs “by itself.” A second rule could establish the reverse relationship.

Verified evidence:

- **7Sage overview:** “necessary” means required; being in the US is required for being in Texas, and absence rules Texas out. [Transcript, lines64–70](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/7sage-curriculum/conditional-overview-Tjdkaq4A-xM/source-transcript.txt:64). Its later example explicitly rejects inferring practicing lawyer from bar passage. [Lines307–322](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/7sage-curriculum/conditional-overview-Tjdkaq4A-xM/source-transcript.txt:307).
- **7Sage relational clarification:** necessary and sufficient describe roles in a particular relationship. A category can play different roles in different relationships. [Dashboard1, lines15–21](</C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/inbox/Dashboard 1.md:15>).
- **LSAT Lab16784:** the left condition requires the right condition. [VTT, lines796–809](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/16784/source.en-US.vtt:796). Having the right condition leaves the left unsettled; missing the right rules the left out. [Lines164–197](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/16784/source.en-US.vtt:164), [240–261](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/16784/source.en-US.vtt:240).
- **Demon sufficient/necessary:** necessary is what must hold whenever sufficient holds. [Exact clip, lines25–27](</C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary-2026-10-03/LSAT Demon  Understanding Sufficient v. Necessary.md:25>).
- **Demon mastering conditionals:** “B is required for A” and “A requires B” express the same relationship. The rule does not establish A as required for B. [Reviewed source, lines36–45](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-mastering-conditional-statements.md:36).
- **Demon abstract conditionals:** absence of Boston leaves Massachusetts open; absence of Massachusetts excludes Boston. [Reviewed source, line27](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals.md:27).

The term is then named, the original anchor revisited, and a four-situation chart sets limits on inference.\\r\\n336: \\r\\n337: The order is important: meaning, prediction, reason, name, comparison. The flip-and-negate shortcut appears later, after the reader has a reason to believe the result.\\r\\n338: \\r\\n339: **Transfer:** preserve this order when contraposition is actually in scope. Do not rush the full procedure into the opening definition merely because it appears early in this source.\\r\\n396: |---|---|---|---|\\r\\n397: | **What a conditional says** | A statement makes one condition enough to require another. It does not establish that either condition occurs. | Plain definition, purpose, one stated rule, one case, one tempting reverse. | Decide what the given rule and fact establish; explain the limit. |\\r\\n398: | **Why it matters on the LSAT** | A conclusion can rely on the direction of a rule or on a missing connection. Reversing a relationship can support the wrong answer. | Keep the beginner example; show one supported conclusion and one unsupported inference. | Choose the justified conclusion and name the connection the other answer would require. |\\r\\n399: | **Sufficient** | Enough to establish the necessary condition under this rule; not the only possible way unless stated. | Same anchor, “enough for what?”, present-case explanation, absence leaves the other condition open. | Find the complete sufficient idea and say what it establishes. |\\r\\n400: | **Necessary** | Required for the sufficient condition; presence alone does not establish the sufficient condition. | Same anchor, identify what must be there, compare requirement with guarantee. | Identify the requirement; reject an unsupported reverse with a reason. |\\r\\n401: | **Translation and diagramming** | The diagram preserves the whole relationship, including conditions and qualifications. | Ordinary meaning, indicator, complete ideas, placement, English readback. Introduce later operations when their prerequisites are taught. | Construct a diagram in meaningful steps and compare it with the whole sentence. |\\r\\n402: | **Group 1** | Joshua\'s Group 1 expressions identify the sufficient idea; sentence order can vary. | Teach a simple expression first, reuse meaning across variants, then alter position and scope. | Lesson, guided translation, fresh independent items, explained feedback. |\\r\\n403: | **Group 2** | Joshua\'s Group 2 expressions identify the necessary idea; target and force must be read in context. | Teach the requirement first, compare “if” with “only if,” then develop each expression\'s target and nuances. | Separate Group 2 practice, then a controlled Group 1/2 comparison when both are learned. |\\r\\n404: \\r\\n450: |---|---|\\r\\n451: | “Ignore the conditional” when sufficient is absent or necessary is present. | For this one rule and fact, no new conclusion about the other condition follows. Never teach that it disappears. |\\r\\n452: | Necessary has to happen “at some point.” | A conditional is not necessarily a time sequence or causal claim. Equivalent formulations and other supplied rules still matter. State the immediate inference limits precisely. |\\r\\n454: | Required words are described as obligations. | Preserve modality. “Interviewees must bring ID” can assert an obligation, not prove compliance. ## assistant

Use this lead:

> **Necessary means required.** In a conditional relationship, the necessary condition is what the sufficient condition requires. Whenever the sufficient condition is true, the necessary condition must be true too.

Then immediately return to the anchor:

> If you are enrolled in law school, you are a student.
>
> Being a student is required for law-school enrollment. You cannot be enrolled in law school without being a student. That is why being a student is the necessary condition in this relationship.

Move the current paragraph about “required” not establishing “enough” from line277 into the existing history-student comparison. That lets the definition develop before introducing its limit.

The original HTML’s useful contribution is certainty: the requirement must hold when the sufficient condition holds. Its door metaphor and “at some point” wording add less clarity. The selected standard specifically corrects the timing implication.
